newsitem.title: UK: Europe low sulphur straight-run fuel heads to U.S.
newsitem.headline: Europe low sulphur straight-run fuel heads to U.S.

text.p: European low sulphur straight-run fuel oil has been attractive enough in September to be shipped in vast quantities to the U.S., but has found little favour among European buyers, despite historically low prices compared with crude.

A U.S. trader refiner has picked up between 200,000 and 300,000 tonnes of European low sulphur straight-run for its transatlantic operations out of a European total output of between 400,000 and 500,000 tonnes per month.
"We have been buying since mid-September. It's no secret," said a trader at the company who added that prices in the low $120s fob NWE were still workable to the U.S.
On Wednesday prices were assessed around $125-127 fob NWE.

Sellers of low sulphur straight-run have been puzzled about the lack of European buying for a fuel that is used as an alternative to crude as a feedstock, especially since the fob low sulphur straight-run spread against front month benchmark Brent crude is $49 a tonne, its highest level for nearly three years, analysts say.
"I'm absolutely astounded by it. I've rechecked to see if we had our straight-run margins set up right," said a trader at a U.K. refinery.

The wide crack was initiated when tension in the Middle East propelled crude to their highest levels since the Gulf War and pushed other products higher, but gave little backing to low sulphur straight-run.
With European refineries running at near maximum capacity, some analysts feel there was no room to use straight-run.
"They (refiners) do not have the room to take advantage of the (low sulphur straight run) prices," said one analyst.
Another factor contributing to the poor popularity of low sulphur straight-run in September has been the weakness of low sulphur cracked fuel compared with high sulphur cracked material.

"Why buy low sulphur straight-run which will give you weak low sulphur straight-run when it's possible to use high sulphur straight-run and get a better return with your high sulphur cracked residue," said a trader at an oil major.
In addition, a number of traditional European buyers have been engaged in maintenance work at their refineries which knocked demand this month.
"If your refinery is running sweet crude, you may want to optimise operations by using sour (high sulphur) straight-run," the trader said.
